title: What Is Double Brokering? How It Works and How to Stop It
summary: Double brokering is when a carrier passes your load to another carrier without your knowledge. How it happens, warning signs, costs, and pickup checks.
body_markdown:
Double brokering is when a motor carrier accepts a load from a broker and then passes it to another carrier without the shipper's or the broker's knowledge. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) describes it that way, and adds that the carrier that delivers the load often does not get paid \[1\].


For the broker, the problem shows up late. The unpaid carrier calls to ask for its money, a different truck arrives at the dock, or the freight disappears. The check that catches it most directly happens at pickup: compare the truck and driver that arrive with the carrier you booked.


## What double brokering is


FMCSA's description comes from its 2023 broker financial responsibility rule. A carrier "accepts a load from a broker and then transfers the load without the shipper's or original broker's knowledge to another motor carrier who actually delivers the load." The original broker pays the carrier it contracted with, and that carrier "does not pay the second motor carrier" \[1\].


Two federal rules are close to it:


- Only a registered broker may arrange transportation for pay. A person who knowingly arranges freight without broker registration and the required financial security is liable for a civil penalty and "to the injured party for all valid claims incurred without regard to amount." The liability reaches the company and its officers, directors, and principals \[2\]. The current inflation-adjusted penalty for knowingly operating as an unregistered broker is up to $13,676 per violation \[3\].
- A dispatch service that arranges loads for several carriers and allocates traffic among them is not a bona fide agent, and must register as a broker \[4\].


Not every handoff is illegal. Under FMCSA's rules, a carrier that has accepted a load and legally bound itself to transport it is not acting as a broker when it arranges that transportation \[5\]. That is why the broker-carrier agreement matters: it is where you require your written consent before the carrier gives your load to anyone else.


## How double brokering happens


The common pattern runs in five steps \[6\]\[7\]:


1. A scammer registers as a carrier, or uses the identity of a real carrier.
2. The scammer books your load at your rate.
3. The scammer posts the same load again, often at a higher rate, and a second carrier takes it.
4. The second carrier picks up and delivers the freight.
5. The scammer collects from you and does not pay the carrier that hauled the load.


A 2019 federal case shows the money side. The defendant admitted that his group posed as legitimate trucking companies, double brokered loads to legitimate carriers, and cashed fuel-advance checks from brokers. He deposited over 1,000 checks worth $1,171,314.11. "The conspirators did not pay the trucking company that actually transported the goods" \[7\].


The same identity tricks also lead to theft. In April 2026, federal prosecutors in Boston indicted a man for a cargo theft conspiracy. According to the indictment, the group sent shippers emails "made to appear as though they were being sent by legitimate trucking carrier companies," and took loads that included $325,000 of frozen snow crab and more than $430,000 of cologne \[8\]. The charges are allegations.


FMCSA says fraud and identity theft occur when someone uses another carrier's U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) number without authorization, or acts as a broker without registering \[9\]. Since May 19, 2026, FMCSA's new registration system, Motus, has checked identity with government-issued IDs and facial scans \[15\]. FMCSA said it will verify all new applicants, and existing registrants the first time they use the system \[10\]. A stolen identity is harder to register now, but a registered carrier can still pass your load to someone else.


## Warning signs of double brokering


FMCSA and the Transportation Intermediaries Association (TIA) list these signs \[6\]\[9\]:


Warning sign Where to look Source


Recently activated authority FMCSA registration record TIA


Phone number differs from the one in SAFER FMCSA SAFER FMCSA


Dispatch will not give you the driver's cell number Booking call TIA


Carrier will not accept tracking Tracking request TIA


Quick pay request from a carrier you have not used Carrier onboarding TIA


Free email account, or a domain one letter off the carrier's Rate confirmation email TIA


Many recent address changes, or a P.O. box address FMCSA registration record TIA


Name and USDOT number on the truck differ from the booked carrier Truck door at pickup FMCSA, TIA


FMCSA also warns that "even insurance certificates can be fraudulent" \[9\]. Confirm insurance with the insurer or agent, not only with the certificate the carrier sends.


Most of these signs show up at booking. Only the last one shows which carrier has your freight.


## What double brokering costs a broker


- You can pay twice. When the hauling carrier is not paid, it contacts the broker or shipper on the bill of lading. TIA notes that "often double payment (to the scammer and the motor carrier) would be required" \[6\].
- You can lose the freight. A party that can take your load without your knowledge can also take it to a place you did not choose \[8\].
- Your carrier vetting no longer covers the load. You checked one carrier, and a different one is on the road. TIA says double brokering "can also cause liability challenges making it harder to determine who is liable for the crash" \[6\]. Since the Supreme Court's May 2026 decision in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, a broker can face state negligent-selection claims after a crash \[11\].
- Your bond can be at risk. Since January 16, 2026, if a broker's available financial security falls below $75,000 and is not replenished within 7 calendar days, FMCSA suspends the broker's operating authority \[12\].


Ask your insurance agent how your contingent cargo policy treats a load that a carrier passed to another carrier without your consent.


Enforcement is slow. In 2024, FMCSA told Congress that since a 2019 administrative law ruling, it "has lacked the statutory authority to assess civil penalties administratively for unauthorized brokerage violations." It must go through federal court instead \[13\].


## How to stop double brokering at pickup


Carrier vetting at booking tells you about the carrier you contracted. Pickup is where you see the carrier that actually showed up. FMCSA's advice is direct: "Confirm the name and numbers on the truck that shows up to load are the same as the one with which you contracted" \[9\].


On each load with a higher risk, check:


1. The USDOT number on the truck door matches the booked carrier.
2. The driver's commercial driver's license (CDL) matches the driver the carrier assigned.
3. The tractor and trailer plates match what dispatch gave you. FMCSA suggests asking your customer to record the plates \[9\].
4. The phone number you call is the one in SAFER, not only the one in the email \[9\].
5. Sensitive pickup details, such as the pickup number, go out only after the checks pass.


When a check fails, hold the load and call the booked carrier at its SAFER number. Ask who the driver is and whose truck it is. Record what failed, who reviewed it, and what they decided.


Indemni can hold back selected details of the rate confirmation (rate con), such as the pickup number, until the assigned driver passes verification. The driver takes a photo of the truck door, Indemni reads the USDOT number and compares it with the driver's carrier, and the full rate con goes out only after that check and the driver's other checks pass \[14\].[See how Indemni stops double brokering](https://www.indemni.com/platform/rate-con-secure-release#faq-how-does-indemni-stop-double-brokering)


If a check fails, the details stay hidden and your team sees which check failed. They can ask the carrier for a different driver, or review the result and release the rate con themselves \[14\].


Carrier lookup and driver verification sit on the same load. Carrier lookup shows the carrier you booked, and driver verification shows the driver and truck that arrive, so you see it when the two do not match \[14\].[See how carrier lookup connects to pickup](https://www.indemni.com/platform/carrier-lookup#faq-how-does-this-connect-to-the-driver-who-shows-up)


## What to do when you find a double-brokered load


1. Stop the release of pickup details if the truck has not loaded.
2. Call the booked carrier at the number in SAFER.
3. Talk to the carrier that has the freight, and confirm where it is going.
4. Keep the rate con, emails, call log, and pickup photos with the load.
5. Report it. FMCSA points to its National Consumer Complaint Database, the FMCSA Contact Center at 1-800-832-5660, and the USDOT Office of Inspector General hotline \[9\].
